questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}+6y=12.
$$

Find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.

${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of our inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha ,
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)=0.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
0+6\alpha =12\,⟹\,\alpha =2.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=2.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=-4x-5.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-4x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\alpha +4(\alpha x+\beta )=-4x-5
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
4\alpha x+(\alpha +4\beta )=-4x-5
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4\alpha =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \alpha +4\beta =-5\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,\,\beta =-1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-x-1.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-4x}-x-1.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=-{x}^{2}+2x-3.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $, and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma ,$  we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
(2\alpha x+\beta )+(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=-{x}^{2}+2x-3
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
\alpha {x}^{2}+(2\alpha +\beta )x+(\beta +\gamma )=-{x}^{2}+2x-3
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\alpha =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 2\alpha +\beta =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \beta +\gamma =-3\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,\beta =4,\gamma =-7.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-{x}^{2}+4x-7.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}-{x}^{2}+4x-7.
$$

$$

Given that the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{′}-6y=12x+8
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}=A{e}^{6x},$ solve the initial value problem.

questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-6{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{6x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\alpha -6(\alpha x+\beta )=12x+8
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
-6\alpha x+(\alpha -6\beta )=12x+8
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha =12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \alpha -6\beta =8\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-2,\,\beta =-\frac{5}{3}.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-2x-\frac{5}{3}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{6x}-2x-\frac{5}{3}.
$$

Now, we can find the constant $A$ using the initial conditions.

Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{6(0)}-2(0)-\frac{5}{3} & =2 \\ A-\frac{5}{3} & =2 \\ A & =\frac{11}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=\frac{11}{3}\,{e}^{6x}-2x-\frac{5}{3}.
$$

questions.problem:

$$
{y}^{′}+y=3,\,y(0)=-1
$$

Given that the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{′}+y=3
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}=A{e}^{-x},$ solve the initial value problem.

questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a constant. Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a constant, i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\beta ,
$$

where $\beta $ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

To find the value of $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
0+\beta =3
$$

Solving for $\beta $ gives $\beta =3.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}+3.
$$

Now, we can find the constant $A$ using the initial conditions.

Substituting $y(0)=-1$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{0}+3 & =-1 \\ A+3 & =-1 \\ A & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-4\,{e}^{-x}+3.
$$
